newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- JULY 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- JULY 7.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--The government is prepared to make three commitments in its effort to convince employers and unionists to sign a new social contract that will allow Greece entry into economic and monetary union in 2001. The commitments are: a three-year freeze on tariffs for services by public utilities; index-linking of income tax scales; and a reduction in taxation of firms.

--Greek industry is joining forces with the foreign and development ministries to prepared an assault of "economic diplomacy" in the Balkans. Leading firms - many already active in the Balkans and from all sectors of economic activity in Greece - will attend a meeting organised by the Federation of Greek Industries (SEV) later this week. The participation of the foreign ministry underlines the significance attritubuted by the government to economic diplomacy and aims at assisting the development and realisation of Greek business plans in the Balkans by recruiting Greek embassies and commercial attaches into the effort.

--Anti-seismic guidelines for the new international airport at Spata may mean a revision of the contract following the government's insistence that construction consortium Hochtief comply with new stricter anti-seismic building measures.

--The failure of Katsoulis Securities to meet clients' commitments last week was no surprise to many in the market; in fact, the same is believed to be in store for another four to five securities firms.

--An increase in indicators used by the tax department to calculate minimum income brackets for firms and self-employed professionals, noted in 1997 tax returns, will mean an increased tax bill for some 800,000 small and medium-size enterprises.
--Industries involved in the production of consumables have returned the highest profits inm 1996, almst half of the profits of the 500 largest Greek profit-making industries.

--Western Europeans, Greece's traditional market for tourists, have gradually been abandoning Greece as their holiday destination, although Eastern Europeans have been quick to fill their shoes. From 1994-1996, Greece lost an enormous amount of foreign exchange, which, National Greek Tourist Organisation Secretary-General Nikos Skoulas says, can be turned around with the right measures.

--Intracom, Greece's leading telecoms firm, is considering investing in the US, as part of its goal to be nearer to the centre of technological developments. The firms investment programme for the next three years totals 50 billion drachmas.

--Ministers are squabbling over the colossal amount of 600 billion drachmas of European Community funds that has not been absorbed by the programmes and projects it was originally destined for: the amount will now be allocated to other public programmes and talks between ministers losing funds for their ministries and those gaining must be finished by mid-July. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
